links.text: Nottingham Corporation Tramways built the depot in 1900 when it carried the Carrington tram line on up Mansfield Road to Winchester Street. Trams ran until 6 September 1936, when buses replaced them. Part of the building is now the Samuel Hall pub, named after the man who laid out Sherwood.

The name goes back at least to the 14th century. Thomas Mapurley was under-sheriff of Nottinghamshire from about 1387 and mayor of Nottingham in 1402–03. The high ground to the north-east was long known as Mapperley Plains.

In the 1790s Ichabod Wright built Mapperley Hall at the heart of his estate. His grandson, Colonel Charles Ichabod Wright, began selling land for houses in 1873, but most of the estate was released only in 1903; some 163 houses were approved in Mapperley Park between 1906 and 1914.
T. C. Hine designed the Coppice Hospital, a hospital on the hill off Ransom Road, built in 1857–59. It closed in 1985, and the building is now flats.

In August 1842 a meeting of more than two thousand in the Market Place voted to stop work until the People's Charter became law. The magistrates banned further meetings, and for days troops and police broke up gatherings across the town. On 23 August Chartists from Hucknall, Bulwell, Arnold, Basford and other places met on the common on Mapperley Hills; the 2nd Dragoon Guards were sent, and when the crowd, sitting on the grass to eat, would not disperse, Colonel Rolleston had about four hundred arrested. As they were marched into the town, a crowd stoned the soldiers and police. About fifty went for trial, some getting hard labour. Afterwards the town's workers turned instead against the Corn Laws and the price of bread. The pin is approximate.

The clay of the high ground fed some of the area's biggest brickworks. In the 1860s Edward Gripper mechanised them, with Hoffmann kilns, and brickmaking went on until 1969. Mapperley bricks are said to have built St Pancras station, and so, people said, Nottingham once stood on Mapperley Plains. The pin is approximate.

St Jude's on Woodborough Road opened in 1877 on land given by the Wright family, as a daughter church of St Ann's. Its chancel came in 1893 and its aisles in 1916, and it became a parish of its own on 9 November 1926.

George Thomas Hine designed the Nottingham Borough Lunatic Asylum, opened in August 1880 with its wards along one long corridor. It was extended in 1889, joined the NHS as Mapperley Hospital in 1948, and closed in December 1994. The north end is now Duncan Macmillan House, the local NHS trust's headquarters, and the south end, Nightingale House, is flats.

Domesday Book, in 1086, calls it Carentune. For centuries it was a small township in the manor and parish of Gedling, home to farmers and framework knitters.

The textile trade and the railways grew Carlton in the 19th century: its population climbed steadily from the 1840s, and by 1850 it had become a suburb with its own houses, churches and schools. The tram line from Nottingham reached it in 1914.
Henry Herbert, 4th Earl of Carnarvon, built the church of St Paul, which was consecrated in 1885. It is listed Grade II.

Her life of her husband, John Hutchinson, written for her family, was printed in 1806. She died at Owthorpe in 1681.

William Howitt, born in Heanor, made his home in Nottingham with Mary Howitt and was an alderman of the town, before they moved to Esher in 1837. In 1852 he sailed to Melbourne with two of his sons.

Mary Howitt married William Howitt in 1821, and by 1823 they were living in Nottingham, on Timber Hill, now South Parade, next to Smith's Bank, for over twelve years. She wrote The Spider and the Fly and translated Hans Christian Andersen's tales.
Ruth Bryan (1805–1860) came to Nottingham as a child with her father, a minister. She lived at 18 High Pavement and kept a detailed diary from 1822.

Sarah Gray, Nottingham's first woman GP, lived and practised at 21 Regent Street. At the Women's Hospital from 1899 she was refused charge of in-patients; in 1921 she became the first president of the Nottingham Medico-Chirurgical Society.

Mary Kendrick, the tidal engineer who led the studies of river levels and silt for the Thames Barrier, grew up on Curzon Street, where her father was a haulage contractor. She later kept the Mersey navigable as its Acting Conservator.

Ann Morley, a businesswoman, built this house in 1750, a rare Georgian town house built by a woman. The Nottingham School of Design opened here in 1843, and in 1854 the lace merchant George Gill made it the People's Hall, an institute for working men.

William "Bendigo" Thompson, born in Nottingham on 11 October 1811, won the heavyweight championship of England in 1839. He died in 1880 and was buried in St Mary's burial ground, under a tomb with a crouching lion. The city of Bendigo in Australia is indirectly named after him.

Arthur Shrewsbury, born in New Lenton in 1856, scored his first century at Trent Bridge in 1876 and captained England seven times, the last professional to do so until Len Hutton. Asked whom he would most like in his side, W. G. Grace said: "Give me Arthur."

Harry Cursham was born in Wilford on 27 November 1859. In the FA Cup he scored 49 goals in 44 games for Notts County, the competition's individual scoring record, and for England 5 goals in 8 games; he also played two first-class cricket matches for Nottinghamshire. He died on 6 August 1941. The pin is approximate.
Tinsley Lindley, who played for Nottingham Forest and England and became a county court judge, lived here with his family at 14 Park Terrace.
Herbert Kilpin, a butcher's son, grew up here with nine older siblings, at what was then 129 Mansfield Road. He became the main founding father of AC Milan.

James Iremonger was born in Norton, in the East Riding of Yorkshire, on 5 March 1876, and played for Wilford's football club in 1893. He played for Nottingham Forest from 1895 to 1910, won two England caps in 1901–02, played cricket for Nottinghamshire from 1899 to 1914 and coached the county from 1921 to 1938. His brother was Albert Iremonger, the Notts County goalkeeper. He died in Nottingham on 25 March 1956.
Born in Wilford, the 6 ft 5 in goalkeeper played 564 matches for Notts County. In the 1940s he ran the Ferry Inn.

Harold Larwood, born at Nuncargate in 1904, played for Nottinghamshire from 1924 and bowled for England in the Bodyline series. He moved to Australia in 1950; Trent Bridge named the Larwood and Voce Stand after him and Bill Voce in 1985.
Bill Voce, born at Annesley Woodhouse in 1909, walked from Hucknall to Trent Bridge hoping for a trial. With Harold Larwood he bowled Bodyline for England, and he later became the county's coach.

Viv Anderson was born in Clifton on 29 July 1956. In ten years at Nottingham Forest, from 1974 to 1984, he played 328 times and won the European Cup twice. In November 1978, against Czechoslovakia, he became the first black footballer to play for England's senior men's team.

Nellie Crocker was the suffragettes' organiser in Nottingham from 1909 to 1912, with an office on Carlton Street. After her eighth arrest, for attacking a post office in London, she spent three months of 1912 in Holloway.

Louisa Clarke opened a day and boarding school for girls in 1874, at 9 Park Terrace; called Western House, it moved here, to 30 The Ropewalk, in 1890. Rose Feilmann, who wrote "There are fairies at the bottom of my garden", was one of her pupils.

Jessie Batten, a London graduate of 1892, owned Western House school here from 1895. She married in 1910 but kept her own name at work, and retired in 1918.
Louisa May Long (1892–1981), who nursed with the 94 Nottingham VAD at Radcliffe on Trent in the First World War, was Matron of Florence Boot Hall from 1928 to 1946.

Helena Dowson ran Nottingham's suffrage society from 1895 and its shop on Long Row. In 1920 she became the first woman magistrate and a Liberal councillor for the Meadows; a plaque here at the Justice Centre remembers her.

Domesday Book calls the village Aitone. Its church of St Laurence stands east of the Market Place: local tradition dates parts of it to the 11th century and King Cnut, but its oldest parts may be from after the Conquest, in the 12th century. It was a daughter church of Sawley until the 19th century. It is listed Grade II*.
In 1694 the "Great Fire" of Long Eaton destroyed 14 houses and several other buildings in the market place.
Long Eaton stayed a village until the Midland Counties Railway came in 1839. A great railway yard, Toton Sidings, grew up just north of the town, and by 1900 it had more than 10,000 people.

Lace made Long Eaton. High Street Mill dates from 1857, West End Mill of 1882 stands beside the Erewash Canal, and by 1907 the town had almost 1,400 lace machines and more than 4,000 people in the trade.
Harrington Mill, one of the largest lace mills, was built in 1885. It took one and a quarter million bricks to build, and is 167 metres long.

The town's new wealth shows in its Art Nouveau buildings: York Chambers of 1901 and the Midland Counties District Bank of 1903, at 38 and 40 Market Place, and the Carnegie Library on Tamworth Road of 1906, by the same architects, Gorman and Ross. York Chambers and the library are listed Grade II.

Ilkeston was probably founded in the 6th century, and is said to take its name from a founder called Elch. Domesday Book, in 1086, calls it Tilchestune, held mostly by Gilbert de Ghent. Queen Victoria made it a borough in 1887.
Henry III granted Ilkeston its charter in 1252, and its fair is held in the Market Place. Two fairs were joined into one in 1888, and the Charter Fair has been held every October since.

Iron-working at Stanton grew into a huge concern from the 1780s. By the mid-19th century the works made 20,000 tons of iron castings a year, and 2.5 million by 1905. From 1985 the French Saint-Gobain group ran it, and the last casting, in 2007, was an emotional day. The pin is approximate.

Ilkeston once had three stations. The Town station closed to passengers in 1947, the North in 1964 and the Junction in January 1967, leaving the town without a station for fifty years. After a long campaign a new Ilkeston station was approved in 2013 and, delayed by flood works and great crested newts, opened on 2 April 2017. The pin is approximate.
In 1937 finds from a Bronze Age settlement built on piles, from between 1000 and 500 BC, were made near the foot of Clifton Grove. The pin is approximate.
In 1900 the remains of a paved Roman ford, edged with oak posts, were found in the Trent at Wilford. The pin is approximate.
Roman buildings, pottery and coins have been found in Chilwell. It began as a hamlet on the road from Nottingham to Ashby-de-la-Zouch, and is in the Domesday Book of 1086. The pin is approximate.
A 6th-century Anglo-Saxon burial ground has been excavated at Mill Hill, to the north of the old village. The pin is approximate.

In Saxon times the village was known as Addensburgh, and a ferry crossed the Trent here from before 1774. In 1966 a hoard of Roman coins was found on a footpath near the railway and Barrett Lane.

In 868 a Viking army under Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan Ragnarsson took Nottingham and wintered here. Burgred of Mercia and his West Saxon allies laid siege, but made peace and let them go in 869. From 877 the Danes settled, and Nottingham, a town of about 39 acres, became one of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw, until Edward of Wessex took it in 918. King Edmund won the Five Boroughs back for the English in 942.

Between 919 and 924 Edward the Elder had defences and houses built at the south end of Trent Bridge, to guard Nottingham against the Danes. This was the beginning of West Bridgford. In 1086 the Domesday survey recorded it as part of the manor of Clifton.

The Anglo-Saxon cross in St Helen's churchyard dates from around AD 1000, though some put it as early as the 8th century. Its shaft is carved with interlace and a winged figure with a spear, perhaps an archangel or St Luke. Its head was lost in the 18th century; after several moves it came to the churchyard in 1928. Pevsner called it by far the most important pre-Conquest monument in Nottinghamshire, and it is listed Grade I.
Domesday Book, in 1086, calls the village Ernehale. A history of Arnold written in 1913 traces the name back to its Anglo-Saxon settlers, worn down over the centuries into Arnold.
Domesday Book, in 1086, calls the village Baseford; the name holds that of an Anglo-Saxon called Basa. It became part of Nottingham in 1877.
Domesday Book, in 1086, records Bulwell as the village of Buleuuelle. The name probably comes from a spring, the Bull Well, or from an Anglo-Saxon man called Bulla and his well.

The village appears as Calvretone in the Domesday survey of 1086, with a church and a priest. St Wilfrid's Church dates mostly from the 14th century; its nave and tower were rebuilt in 1760–63 and its chancel in 1835, and it was restored in 1881.
Domesday Book, in 1086, calls it Carentune. For centuries it was a small township in the manor and parish of Gedling, home to farmers and framework knitters.
Domesday Book, in 1086, calls it Hochenale. From 1295 until 1915 the town was Hucknall Torkard, after the Torcards, the leading landowners.

Domesday Book calls the village Aitone. Its church of St Laurence stands east of the Market Place: local tradition dates parts of it to the 11th century and King Cnut, but its oldest parts may be from after the Conquest, in the 12th century. It was a daughter church of Sawley until the 19th century. It is listed Grade II*.

Before the Conquest the manor of Wilford belonged to Gode the Countess. In Domesday Book the settlement is named Willesforde, with a fishery, a priest and 23 sokemen. Clifton and Wilford, Peverel lands, passed to the Crown early in Henry II's reign, and the king granted them to Gerbode de Escalt; in Richard I's time they passed to the de Rodes family. Before 1280 Gervase de Clifton obtained both manors from Sir Gerard de Rodes for £30 a year, and a charter of 1280 confirmed the grant. In 1853 Sir J. G. J. Clifton was lord of the manor, owned all its land but the church's glebe, and was patron of the church; in 1870–72 the manor still belonged to Sir R. J. Clifton.

From about 1285 the area was known as Walker Gate, after the "walking", or treading, of cloth to thicken it. Nottingham's wool trade mattered: between 1343 and 1345 the price of wool in its market was the standard for all of England.

The district takes its name from a spring once thought to heal. It was recorded in 1301 as the Brodewell, and was also called Robin Hood's Well; in 1500 monks built a chapel beside it and dedicated it to St Ann. A spired cover put over it in 1856 was pulled down in 1887 for the railway, and the site was later built over by the Gardeners pub.

The name goes back at least to the 14th century. Thomas Mapurley was under-sheriff of Nottinghamshire from about 1387 and mayor of Nottingham in 1402–03. The high ground to the north-east was long known as Mapperley Plains.

The village's older name was Barton in the Beans, after the beans grown here; fabis is Latin for beans. A ferry crossed the Trent from here to Attenborough from before 1774. Today Fairham, a new district, is being built in the parish beside Clifton.

Giltbrook's name is thought to come from the Old English Gylden Broc, the golden brook, after the stream that runs down from the fields north of where IKEA now stands. A retail park was built beside IKEA in 2008.
Gotham means "goat home" in Old English. Washington Irving gave the name "Gotham" to New York in his Salmagundi Papers of 1807, and Bill Finger in turn named Batman's city Gotham City.

Robin Hood is the legendary outlaw of English folklore, a skilled archer said to rob the rich to give to the poor. The earliest ballads are usually thought to be set in the 13th or 14th century, and the first clear mention of Robin Hood rhymes comes in Piers Plowman, in the 1370s. In the stories he lives in Sherwood Forest, and his enemy is the Sheriff of Nottingham. James Woodford's bronze of him at Nottingham Castle was unveiled in 1952 and listed Grade II in 2018.

The first written record of a royal hunting lodge at Bestwood is from 1286, in the reign of Edward I. Charles II and Nell Gwyn visited it, and in 1682 he leased the lodge to her. Their son, Charles Beauclerk, Earl of Burford, was made Duke of St Albans in 1684, and Bestwood passed down through his descendants.

In 1330 Roger Mortimer, 1st Earl of March, ruled England with Queen Isabella as regents for her young son, Edward III. That October Sir William Montagu led Edward's men up a secret tunnel through the castle rock to a door high in the castle, and they seized Mortimer; he was sent to the Tower of London and hanged a month later. The long passage to the bottom of the rock is known as Mortimer's Hole.

When the House of Lords threw out the Second Reform Bill on 8 October 1831, rioting broke out in Nottingham and a crowd burned the castle, which belonged to the Duke of Newcastle, an opponent of reform. Three men were hanged; the Duke refused to restore the castle, and its burnt shell stood on the rock for years.

The Park began as a wooded deer park on the west side of Nottingham Castle, hunted while the castle belonged to the Crown. In 1663 William Cavendish, 1st Duke of Newcastle, bought the ruined castle together with its park, and the land stayed with his successors for almost three centuries.
In August 1642 Charles I raised his standard outside Nottingham Castle, at the opening of the English Civil War.

Henry Ireton, eldest son of German Ireton of Attenborough, was baptised in St Mary's Church here on 3 November 1611. He fought for Parliament at Edgehill in October 1642. On the night before Naseby, in June 1645, he surprised the Royalist army; the next day he was wounded and captured, and Cromwell later freed him. He married Bridget, Cromwell's eldest daughter, was one of the commissioners who signed the death warrant of Charles I, and died of disease outside Limerick on 26 November 1651.

A church of St Nicholas stood here from the 11th or 12th century. In the Civil War, Royalists took its tower and fired on the castle's garrison, so in 1643 the castle's governor, Colonel John Hutchinson, had it destroyed. For 28 years there was no church here; the brick church standing today was begun in 1671 and finished in 1678.

The Royalists of Newark raided again and again. Sir Charles Lucas broke into the town in January 1644 and tried to set it on fire, and in April 1645 a party from Newark took the fort at Trent Bridge. Each time Hutchinson won back what was lost, and each demand that he surrender the castle he answered with fresh defiance.
Henry Poole's bronze of the airman Albert Ball, with an allegorical female figure, in the castle gardens. Ball was killed on 7 May 1917, and the memorial was unveiled in 1921; it is listed Grade I.

By 1310–11 Shelford's church belonged to an Augustinian priory here. After Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries, the Stanhopes acquired the priory, in 1537, and with it the church. Lady Anne Stanhope's tomb, by Gabriel Royle, was put up after her death in 1588, and the family vault is dated 1677. In 1877–78 Lord Carnarvon paid for Ewan Christian to restore the church.

In 1589 William Lee of Calverton invented the stocking frame, a machine that knitted. Legend has it that Elizabeth I refused him a patent. The trade grew here, and from 1728 Nottingham was one of its main centres.

After William Lee died in about 1614 the stocking frame spread slowly: in 1644 London had some 400 to 500 frames and Nottinghamshire about 150. In 1728 Nottingham's magistrates refused the authority of the London Company of Framework Knitters, and the town became a chief centre of the trade. England had some 14,000 frames by 1750, and in 1758 Jedediah Strutt's "Derby rib" let them knit ribbing. Short of yarn, the knitters looked for ways to spin cotton here.
Richard Arkwright's first cotton mill opened in Nottingham in 1768, its machines turned by horses. By 1772 it had four storeys and 300 workers.

In 1778 George, James and John Robinson took a 56-year lease from Frederick Montagu to build cotton mills on the Leen. With Castle Mill, Grange Farm, Middle Mill and Forge Mill, and the dam and Moor Pond that fed them, they employed around 800 people, many of them apprentices brought from the St Marylebone workhouse in London. In 1785 James Robinson bought a Boulton and Watt engine for the mill at Bestwood, said to be the first rotative steam engine in a cotton mill anywhere. Spinning had stopped by 1828, and most of the buildings were taken down in the 1850s.

links.text: The mill owner John Hawksley built a large cotton mill here, working before the end of 1791 with a 60-horsepower engine, and laid out Arnot Hill Park in about 1792 as a setting for his house. His son Thomas Hawksley, born at Arnot Hill House in 1807, became the engineer who gave Nottingham clean water. The house is listed Grade II.
The Luddite movement began in Arnold on 11 March 1811. Across Nottinghamshire the frame-breakers went after the "wide" knitting frames used to make cheap goods.

In about 1829 cottages were built for Ruddington's framework knitters, who worked at hand frames in workshops behind them; the workshops date from about 1840. All are listed, and together they now make up the Framework Knitters' Museum.
During the Reform riots of 1831, Lowe's Silk Mill in Beeston was burnt on 11 October, the day after Nottingham Castle, and the same day the riots ceased.
Victorian Bulwell lived by the Leen. Glove-making, begun in about 1840, employed some 700 people until 1864, and by 1853 there were three bleachworks along the river.

The Leen's clean water brought the bleachers. A directory of 1853 counted eight bleaching works in Basford, with many stocking frames and bobbin-net machines, and a population that had grown from 2,124 to 10,093 by 1851.

Plaque by Southern Broxtowe Blue Plaque Group: “George Henry Hurt 1874-1934. Started his hand-frame knitting business here in 1912. Originally this building was a seed warehouse built c.1781 for John Pearson nurseryman.”

John Leavers lived here, at Canning Circus, where a plaque calls him the inventor of the Leavers lace machine, in 1813. He improved John Heathcoat's lace machine, and in 1821 emigrated to Grand-Couronne in Normandy.

Built from 1854 to designs by Thomas Chambers Hine for Thomas Adams, a Quaker lace manufacturer, and opened in 1855 as his lace showroom and warehouse, with a chapel for the workers in the basement. Inspectors thought it a model example of its kind; since 1999 it has been part of Nottingham College.
Harrington Mill, one of the largest lace mills, was built in 1885. It took one and a quarter million bricks to build, and is 167 metres long.
Plaque by Southern Broxtowe Blue Plaque Group: “Site of SWISS MILLS 1886-1984 / Built by the POLLARD family / Manufacturers of high quality lace in Beeston for 100 years”

Lace made Long Eaton. High Street Mill dates from 1857, West End Mill of 1882 stands beside the Erewash Canal, and by 1907 the town had almost 1,400 lace machines and more than 4,000 people in the trade.

The congregation went back to 1690 and became Unitarian in 1802. In 1876 it built this chapel, to designs by Stuart Colman. Worship ended in 1982; the chapel then housed a lace museum, and it is now a Pitcher & Piano.

Garners Hill, said to be the oldest site in Nottingham, once held cave dwellings, a Saxon fort and a medieval town hall, until the Victorians cleared it for a railway line. On 14 November 2009 an art centre designed by Caruso St John opened here, its walls embossed with a Nottingham lace pattern.

After a poor harvest in 1766, food was dear and people feared shortages. At Goose Fair that October, when Lincolnshire merchants began carting away cheese they had bought, the townspeople tried to stop them; the fair turned to a riot, shops, a warehouse and a boat were looted, and wheels of cheese were rolled down the streets. The mayor could not restore order, and soldiers fired on the crowd, killing William Eggleston, a farmer guarding his own goods. It took several days to bring the town back to order.

Jeremiah Brandreth, born in Wilford, led the Pentrich rising of 1817 and was known as the Nottingham Captain. He was hanged for high treason outside Derby Gaol that November, and then beheaded.

On the night of 9–10 June 1817, men from around Pentrich in Derbyshire set out from South Wingfield to march on Nottingham, led by Jeremiah Brandreth, the Nottingham Captain. At Giltbrook they met a small force of Light Dragoons and scattered. The news that had set them marching was a hoax by William Oliver, a government informer; Brandreth and two others were hanged and beheaded at Derby.

In August 1842 a meeting of more than two thousand in the Market Place voted to stop work until the People's Charter became law. The magistrates banned further meetings, and for days troops and police broke up gatherings across the town. On 23 August Chartists from Hucknall, Bulwell, Arnold, Basford and other places met on the common on Mapperley Hills; the 2nd Dragoon Guards were sent, and when the crowd, sitting on the grass to eat, would not disperse, Colonel Rolleston had about four hundred arrested. As they were marched into the town, a crowd stoned the soldiers and police. About fifty went for trial, some getting hard labour. Afterwards the town's workers turned instead against the Corn Laws and the price of bread. The pin is approximate.

On 23 August 1958 a fight in St Ann's grew into a riot between white and West Indian residents; the police restored order within 90 minutes. A crowd of about 4,000 gathered the following weekend. With the Notting Hill riots a week later, the disturbances led to talks between Caribbean governments and the British government. The pin is approximate.

He lost, and the Conservative John Walter was elected on 4 August 1842; Walter was unseated on petition the next year, and the Liberal Thomas Gisborne won the seat in April 1843. Five years later Nottingham elected the Chartist leader Feargus O'Connor. Where the poll was held is not known.

The Council House, designed by Thomas Cecil Howitt, opened in 1929 on the site of the old Exchange at the head of the Old Market Square. The sculptor Joseph Else named the two stone lions on its steps Agamemnon and Menelaus. Little John, the hour bell in its dome, weighs over 10 tonnes, and its strike can be heard 7 miles away.

The Representation of the People Act, passed on 6 February 1918, gave the vote to women of 30 and over who met a property qualification, and they voted for the first time on 14 December 1918. That November women had also been allowed to stand for Parliament: in Nottinghamshire the first to do so was Violet Markham, at Mansfield, who lost. In 1919 Bridgid Burke-Bloor became the first woman to stand for Nottingham City Council, and in 1920 Helena Dowson and Caroline Harper were its first women councillors. Women won the vote on the same terms as men on 2 July 1928. A hundred years to the day after that first vote, the city unveiled a plaque by a juniper tree in the Arboretum for the suffragette Helen Watts.

Hucknall had been a village of framework knitters. In 1861 the Hucknall Colliery Company sank its Top Pit off Watnall Road, and in 1866 its Bottom Pit off Portland Road, and in under a century Hucknall grew into a market town. The Top Pit closed in 1943 and the Bottom Pit in 1986. A mining memorial in the town centre names both pits. The pin on the former colliery site is approximate.

A branch of the viaduct's railway served the works. They made their last pig iron in March 1931, and in 1934 Thos. W. Ward of Sheffield bought the three furnaces to take them down. The Bestwood Coal and Iron Company's colliery here wound up its coal and lowered its miners with a vertical steam engine of 1873. The pit closed in 1967, but the winding engine house and its engine survive.

Gedling Colliery opened in 1899 and was the area's main employer for almost a century. In the 1960s it dug over a million tonnes of coal a year with 1,400 men, about one in ten of them from the Caribbean, and was known as the "pit of all nations"; 128 men died there over its life. It closed in 1991, and in 2015 its grounds opened as Gedling Country Park.

Calverton Colliery was officially opened on 24 September 1952, and the village grew from 1,304 people in 1951 to 5,658 in 1961. British Coal shut the mine on 19 November 1993; it worked again under RJB Mining until it closed for good in April 1999. The pin is approximate.

The colliery came in the early 1960s: from 1962 hundreds of mining families moved here from Radford's closed pit, and the village grew several times over. The pit worked through the 1984–85 strike and closed in 1993.

Coal has always mattered in Wollaton, from the wagonway onwards. Wollaton Colliery closed in 1965, and houses now cover its ground and that of the old canal: the Torvill and Dean estate. The pin is approximate.

In 1603–1604 Huntingdon Beaumont and Sir Percival Willoughby laid a wooden wagonway from the Strelley coal pits to Wollaton Lane End, its wagons drawn by horses. It is described as the first railway in Britain.

Authorised in 1792 and engineered by William Jessop, the canal opened in 1796 from the Trent to Langley Mill, bringing coal to the town. Railways took its trade; most of the main line was abandoned in 1937.

In 1925 a coal-fired power station opened on the north bank of the Trent. It closed in 1981 and was soon demolished, and the Riverside Retail Park stands on its site.

In 1960 the Central Electricity Generating Board proposed a 2,000 MW power station at Holme Pierrepont, with coal by rail and cooling water from the Trent. A public inquiry of 14 days turned it down, partly because it would have shut off the sand and gravel beneath. The gravel was dug instead, and in 1971 the pits became the National Watersports Centre.

In 1968 a coal-fired power station with eight cooling towers began generating here. It became the last coal-fired power station in Britain, and when it shut in September 2024 it ended 142 years of coal power in the country.

Long Eaton stayed a village until the Midland Counties Railway came in 1839. A great railway yard, Toton Sidings, grew up just north of the town, and by 1900 it had more than 10,000 people.

Between May 1873 and November 1875 Joseph Firbank built a viaduct here for the Great Northern Railway, 43 arches and 1,716 feet long, known locally as Forty Bridges. It was pulled down in 1973 to make way for the A610 bypass.

Built in 1878 to carry the Midland Railway's direct line from Nottingham to Melton Mowbray across the Trent. When the line was abandoned in 1968 the crossing was turned into a road bridge, finished in 1979.

The station opened in 1880 on the Midland Railway's direct line from Nottingham to Melton Mowbray, which let its London expresses avoid Leicester. It closed to passengers in 1941, and its site is now housing. Beyond it the line became the Old Dalby test track, where the Advanced Passenger Train was tried.

Gypsum was dug from Gotham Hill and made into plaster. A branch line about two miles long, opened in March 1899, ran west from the Great Central main line to the works; it closed in the early 1960s and is now a footpath. The pin is approximate.

Nottingham's first station, opened in 1839 by the Midland Counties Railway, stood across Carrington Street; a through station replaced it on this site in 1848. The present building, of red brick and terracotta, was designed by the local architect Albert Edward Lambert and opened on 16 January 1904.

Gedling's railway station closed on 4 April 1960, though coal trains ran to the colliery for decades more. Its building is now a youth centre, and there are plans to reopen the line or make it a cycleway.
Much of the Meadows' pre-1919 terraced housing was demolished to make way for a new development of modern council housing, and the viaduct carrying the Great Central railway came down in 1975.
A shopping centre opened in 1972 on the site of Nottingham Victoria railway station, whose clock tower still stands beside it.
East Midlands Parkway station opened early in 2008 on the Midland Main Line beside Ratcliffe-on-Soar, and is the nearest main-line station to Gotham. The pin is approximate.

Ilkeston once had three stations. The Town station closed to passengers in 1947, the North in 1964 and the Junction in January 1967, leaving the town without a station for fifty years. After a long campaign a new Ilkeston station was approved in 2013 and, delayed by flood works and great crested newts, opened on 2 April 2017. The pin is approximate.

The airfield opened in 1916, and from 1927 Rolls-Royce used it to test its engines. In the Second World War the first P-51 Mustang fitted with a Rolls-Royce Merlin flew from here, and in December 1940 a German prisoner, Franz von Werra, tried to escape by posing as a Dutch pilot and taking a Hurricane. In the early 1950s the works built the "Flying Bedstead", a test rig for vertical take-off, whose first free flight was on 3 August 1954. The flight test centre closed in 1971. The pin is approximate.

Licensed in 1929 and opened in 1930 by Sir Sefton Brancker, it was one of Britain's first municipal aerodromes. In the Second World War it repaired Lancaster bombers; its 18 concrete pillboxes are all listed. The airfield closed on 6 June 2025, sold to the Vistry Group to build 4,000 houses.

Nottingham Corporation Tramways built the depot in 1900 when it carried the Carrington tram line on up Mansfield Road to Winchester Street. Trams ran until 6 September 1936, when buses replaced them. Part of the building is now the Samuel Hall pub, named after the man who laid out Sherwood.

Trolleybuses, buses drawing power from overhead wires, first ran on 10 April 1927 and took over the tram routes one by one; the last tram ran in September 1936. A depot opened on Parliament Street in June 1929 and is still in use. By the end of 1937 the city had 125 trolleybuses, the largest fleet in the country, and at most 157. The last ran on 30 June 1966.
A district built mostly in the 1990s, named after a garden in Poole. Its tram, opened in 2015, runs along a disused railway line.

Trams returned to Nottingham after 68 years when the Nottingham Express Transit network opened in 2004. Hucknall's stop opened on 9 March 2004 with the rest of the first phase, beside the station reopened on 17 May 1993 as part of the Robin Hood Line.

Hine in 1855–56, but at 1 in 12 it was too steep for horses and carriages, so it became a footway. It runs from Tunnel Road to Derby Road, with steps halfway up to Upper College Street.

Fellows Morton & Clayton, who ran the largest fleet of barges and narrowboats in the country, built this canalside depot in 1895. Boats loaded and unloaded at the wharf beside it; the building is now a pub, and listed Grade II.

In 1885 a small bicycle workshop opened in Raleigh Street and gave the company its name; Frank Bowden took it over in 1888.
Frank Bowden took control of a small bicycle maker in Raleigh Street in 1887–88; by 1896 the Raleigh company covered seven and a half acres in Faraday Road.

Alan Sillitoe's 1958 novel became a 1960 film directed by Karel Reisz, with Albert Finney as Arthur Seaton, who works at the Raleigh factory. Much of the exterior location filming took place in Nottingham, and shooting at a Nottingham factory ran two days over schedule and £3,500 over budget.

John Player built his Castle Tobacco Factories in Radford, and the firm's three bonded warehouses, seven to nine storeys high, were finished here in 1939. Tobacco making in Nottingham ended in 2016; the warehouses were demolished, the last in 2022.

John Boot opened a herbalist's shop on Goose Gate in 1849, and his son Jesse was born in the area, into poverty, the next year. After John died in 1860 his widow Mary kept the shop going as M & J Boot. Jesse became a partner at 21, and in 1883 he built a larger store on the same site, the first of the Boots shops; Nottingham Civic Society put up a plaque here in 2015.
In 1908 Jesse Boot built the Dorothy Boot Homes here, 11 homes with a clubroom and a library, for veterans of the Crimean War and the Indian Mutiny.
In 1930–32 the engineer Owen Williams built this factory for Boots' liquid medicines, which gave it its nickname, the "Wets". It is listed Grade I, the largest Grade I-listed structure in Britain.
In 1935–38 Owen Williams built a second factory for Boots, for tablets and lozenges, which gave it its nickname, the "Drys". It too is listed Grade I.

On the night of 8–9 May 1941 the Luftwaffe bombed Nottingham. Firefighters saved St Mary's Church after an incendiary burned through its roof; three Boots factories, in Poplar Street, Island Street and Station Street, were on fire; University College and the Shakespeare Street chapel were hit. The worst loss was at the Co-op bakery on Meadow Lane, where 49 people died. In all, 159 people were killed that night.

The building began in 1839 as a grand Wesleyan chapel on Broad Street. Broadway opened here in 1990, and one of its screens is the only cinema screen designed by Sir Paul Smith.

When the House of Lords threw out the Second Reform Bill on 8 October 1831, rioting broke out in Nottingham and a crowd burned the castle, which belonged to the Duke of Newcastle, an opponent of reform. Three men were hanged; the Duke refused to restore the castle, and its burnt shell stood on the rock for years.

James Shipstone founded the Star Brewery in New Basford in 1852. The red-brick building of 1900 had a red illuminated star on its tower that could be seen for miles. Greenall's of Warrington bought the firm in 1978 and stopped brewing in early 1991; the building now belongs to an auction house.

John Robinson founded the Home Brewery in 1875; its beer mats carried a Robin Hood badge. The family sold it in 1986, and its closure cost some 400 jobs. Its building of 1936 is now Sir John Robinson House, and listed Grade II.

Basford made things for the kitchen and the bathroom. The grocer F. G. Garton started a pickle and sauce factory near his home on Sandon Street and registered the name HP Sauce in 1895. Gerard Brothers opened a soap works in the 1890s; Cussons took it over in 1955, and it closed in 2005. The pin is approximate.
Bulwell's limestone was quarried for building. Stretches of the wall round Wollaton Hall, built in the late 16th century, are of Bulwell stone.

The building of St Ann's may have begun in about 1750, when Charles Morley, who had been sheriff, made brown earthenware in a small factory on Beck Street; his brown beer jugs sold well. The pin is approximate.

Iron-working at Stanton grew into a huge concern from the 1780s. By the mid-19th century the works made 20,000 tons of iron castings a year, and 2.5 million by 1905. From 1985 the French Saint-Gobain group ran it, and the last casting, in 2007, was an emotional day. The pin is approximate.
The King George V Recreation Ground on Standhill Road was once the Standhill Brickworks.

The clay of the high ground fed some of the area's biggest brickworks. In the 1860s Edward Gripper mechanised them, with Hoffmann kilns, and brickmaking went on until 1969. Mapperley bricks are said to have built St Pancras station, and so, people said, Nottingham once stood on Mapperley Plains. The pin is approximate.

The airfield opened in 1916, and from 1927 Rolls-Royce used it to test its engines. In the Second World War the first P-51 Mustang fitted with a Rolls-Royce Merlin flew from here, and in December 1940 a German prisoner, Franz von Werra, tried to escape by posing as a Dutch pilot and taking a Hurricane. In the early 1950s the works built the "Flying Bedstead", a test rig for vertical take-off, whose first free flight was on 3 August 1954. The flight test centre closed in 1971. The pin is approximate.
One of the largest paved squares in the United Kingdom. The two towns were once divided by a wall across it, whose line a stainless steel channel now marks; Goose Fair was held here until 1928.

From about 1285 the area was known as Walker Gate, after the "walking", or treading, of cloth to thicken it. Nottingham's wool trade mattered: between 1343 and 1345 the price of wool in its market was the standard for all of England.

A local law of about 1320 said that only those with covered premises could trade, so Bulwell's market grew up with stalls that were covered while in use and opened out when not. The Market Place has kept much of its old shape.

Before the Old Market Square, Weekday Cross, by the Guild Hall, was the town's main market and its centre. A cross went up here in about 1529–30, and by 1711 people called it "the Pillar". Butter, eggs, pigeons, wild fowl, fruit and fish were sold on Wednesdays and Fridays. The Corporation had the cross pulled down and sold in 1804; Nottingham Civic Society put up a new one in 1993. The Guild Hall's site is now Nottingham Contemporary's.

In 1724–26 the town's Exchange was built in the Market Place to a design by the mayor, Marmaduke Pennell. It held the Corporation's offices, and its Great Hall was used for concerts, elections and balls. It was demolished in 1926 to make way for the Council House.
In the 1930s the city's wholesale fruit and vegetable market moved here from the Old Market Square.
Arnold was a town of hosiery factories, and in 1968 it gained its own market in the town centre.
Henry III granted Ilkeston its charter in 1252, and its fair is held in the Market Place. Two fairs were joined into one in 1888, and the Charter Fair has been held every October since.

A royal charter of 1284 refers to Nottingham's fairs. For centuries Goose Fair was held in the Old Market Square, until in 1928, having outgrown the city centre, it moved to the Forest Recreation Ground. It was cancelled for the Great Plague in 1646 and during the World Wars.

Henry II gave Lenton Priory an eight-day fair for St Martin's Day, which Henry III lengthened to twelve, with tolls paid to the monks for every booth. The fair outlived the priory: in 1584, when servants of Mary, Queen of Scots came, it was a horse fair, and by the 17th century it was known as a great fair for all sorts of horses. In the 19th century farmers and horse dealers still came.

After a poor harvest in 1766, food was dear and people feared shortages. At Goose Fair that October, when Lincolnshire merchants began carting away cheese they had bought, the townspeople tried to stop them; the fair turned to a riot, shops, a warehouse and a boat were looted, and wheels of cheese were rolled down the streets. The mayor could not restore order, and soldiers fired on the crowd, killing William Eggleston, a farmer guarding his own goods. It took several days to bring the town back to order.

John Boot opened a herbalist's shop on Goose Gate in 1849, and his son Jesse was born in the area, into poverty, the next year. After John died in 1860 his widow Mary kept the shop going as M & J Boot. Jesse became a partner at 21, and in 1883 he built a larger store on the same site, the first of the Boots shops; Nottingham Civic Society put up a plaque here in 2015.

In 1964 an American company opened what was called the UK's first major out-of-town superstore on Loughborough Road. In 1966 the young Asda chain took it over, and in 1999 replaced it with a much larger store on the land next to it.
A shopping centre opened in 1972 on the site of Nottingham Victoria railway station, whose clock tower still stands beside it.
Nottingham's racecourse by 1773, and the ground where a club formed in 1865 first played, taking its name from it: Nottingham Forest. Goose Fair has been held here since 1928.

Edward VI granted the land on Hunger Hill to the Corporation of Nottingham in 1551. In 1604–05 it was enclosed and let in plots to 30 burgesses and their widows, an arrangement that lasted until 1842.
In 1836 a cemetery of 18 acres was established at the top of Sion Hill, now Canning Circus, with a gatehouse and almshouses by Samuel Sutton Rawlinson. More than 150,000 people are buried here.

On 11 May 1852 a park laid out under the botanist Samuel Curtis opened here. Its bandstand went up in 1907. The bell from a temple in Canton, taken in the Second Opium War, hung in its war memorial until 1956.
In 1856 the cemetery, laid out by Edwin Patchitt, was consecrated before it was finished. It is also known as the Rock Cemetery and is listed Grade II*.
Tower House is one of the earliest houses in the Park, built to P. F. Robinson's designs between 1827 and 1833. Watson Fothergill later gave it the tower that names it. It is listed Grade II.

Built from 1854 to designs by Thomas Chambers Hine for Thomas Adams, a Quaker lace manufacturer, and opened in 1855 as his lace showroom and warehouse, with a chapel for the workers in the basement. Inspectors thought it a model example of its kind; since 1999 it has been part of Nottingham College.

Built for the lace manufacturers John and William Lambert, who wanted a prestigious theatre for the town, to designs by Charles J. Phipps; its portico of six Corinthian columns closes the view up Market Street. It opened on 25 September 1865 with Sheridan's The School for Scandal, and in 1897 Frank Matcham remodelled its auditorium.

The site was once an inn called the Roebuck. In 1877 a music hall was built here, to designs credited to Edwin Hill, under a high arched glass roof on laminated wooden arches. It took its name from a monument that once stood in the market square, and it is one of the few Victorian music halls to survive.
A hotel on Long Row, rebuilt in 1886–88 by Watson Fothergill and enlarged around 1900. It was demolished in 1970, and a new shop building, first Littlewoods, went up in its place.

Watson Fothergill, born Fothergill Watson, took his mother's family name in 1892 and built his own offices here, on George Street, in 1895. Its front has a statue of a medieval architect and busts of Augustus Pugin and George Edmund Street; it is listed Grade II.

In 1898 Frank Matcham designed and built the Empire Palace of Varieties here. It closed for the last time in 1958 and was demolished for road-widening in 1969. On 27 November 1982 the Royal Concert Hall, designed by the Renton Howard Wood Levin Partnership, opened on the site, with Elton John as its first performer.

In the 1790s Ichabod Wright built Mapperley Hall at the heart of his estate. His grandson, Colonel Charles Ichabod Wright, began selling land for houses in 1873, but most of the estate was released only in 1903; some 163 houses were approved in Mapperley Park between 1906 and 1914.

Mansfield Road was the main road from London to Yorkshire, and a turnpike from 1787. Samuel Hall laid out Sherwood's first streets beside it in 1825; the road was paved and lit in 1879, the year horse trams arrived.

links.text: The first house in the park, built in 1809 opposite the castle gatehouse, was the vicarage of St Mary's. In 1827 the architect Peter Frederick Robinson published a plan for building over the park, and houses began to go up along Park Terrace in about 1829; within three years there were 40 to 50 of them.

The textile trade and the railways grew Carlton in the 19th century: its population climbed steadily from the 1840s, and by 1850 it had become a suburb with its own houses, churches and schools. The tram line from Nottingham reached it in 1914.

Until the Inclosure Act of 1845 the area was open Clay Fields. The Act let the town take 1,068 acres for housing, and by 1880 the streets of terraced houses called New Town were complete. The terraces north of Victoria Park are listed, as a once common kind of house now mostly lost to bombs and clearance.

In 1854 the Duke's estate took on the Nottingham architect Thomas Chambers Hine, to design many of the Park's villas. The roads are still lit by gas lamps, believed to be one of the largest such networks left in Europe.

The Park's villas housed the town's business and public figures: the publisher Richard Allen, who lived at Albert Villa until his death in 1884; the MP Anthony Mundella, for whom Amelia House was built; and Captain Athelstan Popkess, chief constable of Nottingham from 1930 to 1959, at 35 Newcastle Drive.

Wilford parish had 2,769 people in 1891 and about 4,500 by 1901. South Wilford became part of West Bridgford in 1935, and in 1952 Wilford became part of the City of Nottingham. The Silverdale estate was built on its farmland in the late 1950s, and Compton Acres in 1986.

Factories, offices and warehouses filled Radford: Raleigh, once the world's largest bicycle maker, and Player's cigarettes among them. By 1891 the parish had 38,718 people, and on 1 April 1897 it was joined to Nottingham.

Henry Robert Clifton laid the school's cornerstone on 3 November 1871, and it opened in April 1872 with 48 children; a night school for men began a year later. It closed in 1956, when new schools were built on the estate, and is now the village hall.

Built in 1877–81 for University College Nottingham, with the town's library and a natural history museum, and damaged by bombs in the Second World War. D. H. Lawrence studied here to become a teacher; it is now Nottingham Trent University's Arkwright Building.

Built in 1887–88 to designs by Thomas Verity and George Henry Hunt, chosen in a competition judged by Alfred Waterhouse, it replaced the old Guild Hall on Weekday Cross and served as the city's magistrates' court. The council used it as offices until 2010; it has stood largely empty since.
In 1897 Nottingham was made a city, as part of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee celebrations.

Nottingham Victoria, the Great Central and Great Northern railways' station, opened on 24 May 1900 and closed on 4 September 1967. It was demolished except for its clock tower, which still stands at the entrance of the Victoria Centre built on the site.

In 868 a Viking army under Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan Ragnarsson took Nottingham and wintered here. Burgred of Mercia and his West Saxon allies laid siege, but made peace and let them go in 869. From 877 the Danes settled, and Nottingham, a town of about 39 acres, became one of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw, until Edward of Wessex took it in 918. King Edmund won the Five Boroughs back for the English in 942.

Between 919 and 924 Edward the Elder had defences and houses built at the south end of Trent Bridge, to guard Nottingham against the Danes. This was the beginning of West Bridgford. In 1086 the Domesday survey recorded it as part of the manor of Clifton.

The inn was made from two houses and an outbuilding of the late 17th century, and is listed Grade II. Wilford stayed a village until the later 19th century. With woods around it and riverside amenities such as the Ferry Inn, it attracted many visitors from Nottingham. The Notts County goalkeeper Albert Iremonger was its landlord until his death in 1958.
In Saxon times the village was known as Addensburgh, and a ferry crossed the Trent here from before 1774. In 1966 a hoard of Roman coins was found on a footpath near the railway and Barrett Lane.

The village's older name was Barton in the Beans, after the beans grown here; fabis is Latin for beans. A ferry crossed the Trent from here to Attenborough from before 1774. Today Fairham, a new district, is being built in the parish beside Clifton.
In 1900 the remains of a paved Roman ford, edged with oak posts, were found in the Trent at Wilford. The pin is approximate.
In 1937 finds from a Bronze Age settlement built on piles, from between 1000 and 500 BC, were made near the foot of Clifton Grove. The pin is approximate.

In 1947 the Trent flooded 3,000 properties, 86 factories and 28 miles of road in Nottingham, and the city's first flood defence was built that year. Photographs of West Bridgford under water are in Inspire Picture Archive. A new defence along 27 km of the river, from Sawley to Colwick, was finished in 2012.

Built in 1878 to carry the Midland Railway's direct line from Nottingham to Melton Mowbray across the Trent. When the line was abandoned in 1968 the crossing was turned into a road bridge, finished in 1979.

Opened in 1906 to carry water mains across the Trent to the reservoir on Wilford Hill, with a footway over them; it was designed by Arthur Brown of Elliott & Brown. It was restored in 1983 and again in 2008–2010.

In 1958 a bridge opened here to take traffic off Trent Bridge. It was then the longest pre-stressed concrete bridge in the country, and a second bridge beside it, opened in 1972, made the crossing a dual carriageway.

links.text: Dug out of a former gravel works, the centre opened in 1971, and hosted the World Rowing Championships in 1975 and 1986. Its whitewater course was built in 1986.

The mill owner John Hawksley built a large cotton mill here, working before the end of 1791 with a 60-horsepower engine, and laid out Arnot Hill Park in about 1792 as a setting for his house. His son Thomas Hawksley, born at Arnot Hill House in 1807, became the engineer who gave Nottingham clean water. The house is listed Grade II.

In 1881–84 a pumping station was built here to raise drinking water for Nottingham from deep wells. It had two beam engines by James Watt & Co. and an engine house by Marriott Ogle Tarbotton, ornate with cast iron and stained glass. It pumped until 1969 and opened as a museum in 1976.

A Georgian town house was built here in 1752. The Nottingham Subscription Library, founded in 1816, moved in during 1821. In 1836 a meridian line was laid so that the library's longcase clock could keep Nottingham time, 4 minutes and 33 seconds behind Greenwich, and it still does. In 1841 Alfred Barber opened the first photographic studio in the Midlands in its attics.
Shortly after 1807 the baker George Green built a tower mill here. It burned in 1947, was restored and reopened in 1986, and is now part of a science centre.

Built in 1877–81 for University College Nottingham, with the town's library and a natural history museum, and damaged by bombs in the Second World War. D. H. Lawrence studied here to become a teacher; it is now Nottingham Trent University's Arkwright Building.
On 10 July 1928 King George V and Queen Mary opened a building of Portland stone designed by Morley Horder. It now belongs to the University of Nottingham and is listed Grade II.

links.text: Peter Mansfield came to the University of Nottingham in 1964 and developed magnetic resonance imaging here. Just before Christmas 1978 a full-body scanner was installed, and he made the first scan of a live patient. He shared the Nobel Prize in 2003 with Paul Lauterbur.

A legacy from the banker John Key paid for a hospital on part of Nottingham Park. Its first building, designed by John Simpson, was begun on 12 February 1781 and opened with 44 beds in September 1782; John Wesley was an early visitor. In 1844 it took in the hurt when a stand collapsed at a hanging on Garner's Hill, killing twelve. Hine added a storey in 1855, and Alfred Waterhouse's round Jubilee Wing opened in 1900. It closed in 1992, its work moved to the Queen's Medical Centre.

It was extended in 1889, joined the NHS as Mapperley Hospital in 1948, and closed in December 1994. The north end is now Duncan Macmillan House, the local NHS trust's headquarters, and the south end, Nightingale House, is flats.

Viscount Chetwynd built the factory from 1915 to fill shells with explosive; it filled some 19 million during the First World War. On 1 July 1918 eight tons of TNT exploded, killing 134 people. The site is now Chetwynd Barracks.
Plaque by Southern Broxtowe Blue Plaque Group: “The Chilwell Explosion 1st July 1918. Killed 139 people at the nearby No.6 Shell Filling Factory. Albert Hall Chief Engineer, a survivor lived here.”

Henry Ireton, eldest son of German Ireton of Attenborough, was baptised in St Mary's Church here on 3 November 1611. He fought for Parliament at Edgehill in October 1642. On the night before Naseby, in June 1645, he surprised the Royalist army; the next day he was wounded and captured, and Cromwell later freed him. He married Bridget, Cromwell's eldest daughter, was one of the commissioners who signed the death warrant of Charles I, and died of disease outside Limerick on 26 November 1651.
Henry Poole's bronze of the airman Albert Ball, with an allegorical female figure, in the castle gardens. Ball was killed on 7 May 1917, and the memorial was unveiled in 1921; it is listed Grade I.

On 11 November 1927 a memorial designed by the City Engineer Thomas Wallis Gordon was unveiled on land beside the Trent given by Sir Jesse Boot. It remembers the men of Nottingham who died in both World Wars.

Licensed in 1929 and opened in 1930 by Sir Sefton Brancker, it was one of Britain's first municipal aerodromes. In the Second World War it repaired Lancaster bombers; its 18 concrete pillboxes are all listed. The airfield closed on 6 June 2025, sold to the Vistry Group to build 4,000 houses.

Ruddington's station on the Great Central Railway opened on 15 March 1899. From 1940 a depot was built here to fill and store ammunition, and it closed in 1983. The station had closed in 1963, and the Nottingham Heritage Railway now runs trains on the line. The rest of the depot's land is a business park and Rushcliffe Country Park.
In 1941 a German bomber dropped a line of bombs across Lady Bay. New houses went up on the bomb sites in the 1950s and 1960s, and Pinders Ponds, to the east, are thought to be flooded bomb craters.

Around 1361 Gervase de Wilford is thought to have founded a church here, and the building dates from the late 14th century; it was restored in 1890–92 by Naylor and Sale. Inside are two memorials to the poet Henry Kirke White, who drew much inspiration from Wilford and Clifton.
The stone statue of Feargus O'Connor, by J. B. Robinson of Derby, went up in the Arboretum in 1859: the Chartist leader whom Nottingham had elected its MP in 1847. It is listed Grade II.

The Arboretum's bell tower is a war memorial to the 59th (2nd Nottinghamshire) Regiment of Foot, designed by Marriott Ogle Tarbotton in 1862–63. Its cupola held a bell that British troops took from a temple in Canton during the Second Opium War, until the bell went to the regimental museum in 1956. Two of the cannon beside it were taken at Sebastopol in the Crimean War; the other two are copies.

Sir Robert Juckes Clifton, of the Clifton family across the river, was elected MP for Nottingham in 1861 and died of typhoid in 1869, aged 42. The Wilford Toll Bridge he had planned opened the next year, and in 1883 William Philip Smith's stone statue of him was put up at its northern end. It is listed Grade II.

links.text: Robin Hood is the legendary outlaw of English folklore, a skilled archer said to rob the rich to give to the poor. The earliest ballads are usually thought to be set in the 13th or 14th century, and the first clear mention of Robin Hood rhymes comes in Piers Plowman, in the 1370s. In the stories he lives in Sherwood Forest, and his enemy is the Sheriff of Nottingham. James Woodford's bronze of him at Nottingham Castle was unveiled in 1952 and listed Grade II in 2018.

Brian Clough managed Nottingham Forest from January 1975 to May 1993. Under him the club won the League in 1977–78 and the European Cup in 1979 and 1980. Les Johnson's statue of him, at the corner of King Street and Queen Street, was unveiled by his widow Barbara on 6 November 2008.

This was boggy ground on the edge of the medieval town, where the Franciscan friary of Greyfriars stood until it was closed in 1539. After large-scale slum clearance, the Broad Marsh shopping centre was officially opened on 25 March 1975. It closed in 2020 and was left partially demolished; caves found beneath it became part of the City of Caves. In 2025 Homes England bought the site to build homes.

The street was first called Vault Lane, after the great rock cellars under the house where it met Low Pavement, and later Parkyn Lane. It took its present name about 1620 from Alderman Drury, a wealthy shoemaker who lived in that house, Vault Hall. Traffic once had to climb the cliff to the old town by Malin Hill, the Long Stairs and Hollow Stone; it found the slope of Drury Hill, up from Narrow Marsh, much easier, and the street became the town's chief business thoroughfare. When carts and carriages came into use in the 17th century it proved too narrow, and Hollow Stone was eased to become a main way into the town.

At its narrowest the street was only 4 feet 10 inches wide, and a postern gate stood at its top when the town was walled. It was demolished in the 1960s, despite protests, for the Broad Marsh shopping centre.

In 1724–26 the town's Exchange was built in the Market Place to a design by the mayor, Marmaduke Pennell. It held the Corporation's offices, and its Great Hall was used for concerts, elections and balls. It was demolished in 1926 to make way for the Council House.

Methodists met in Nottingham from about 1740, in rooms here and there, and in 1782 moved to Hockley Chapel on Goose Gate. When the New Connexion split from the Wesleyans in 1797 and took that chapel, the Wesleyans bought land in Halifax Place and opened a chapel for 1,600 on 2 December 1798. Its successor of 1847 had the highest ceiling of any Wesleyan chapel in England; it closed in 1930 and was pulled down in 1966.
A hotel on Long Row, rebuilt in 1886–88 by Watson Fothergill and enlarged around 1900. It was demolished in 1970, and a new shop building, first Littlewoods, went up in its place.

Nottingham Victoria, the Great Central and Great Northern railways' station, opened on 24 May 1900 and closed on 4 September 1967. It was demolished except for its clock tower, which still stands at the entrance of the Victoria Centre built on the site.

During the Reform riots of 1831, Lowe's Silk Mill in Beeston was burnt on 11 October, the day after Nottingham Castle, and the same day the riots ceased.

John Player built his Castle Tobacco Factories in Radford, and the firm's three bonded warehouses, seven to nine storeys high, were finished here in 1939. Tobacco making in Nottingham ended in 2016; the warehouses were demolished, the last in 2022.

The district takes its name from a spring once thought to heal. It was recorded in 1301 as the Brodewell, and was also called Robin Hood's Well; in 1500 monks built a chapel beside it and dedicated it to St Ann. A spired cover put over it in 1856 was pulled down in 1887 for the railway, and the site was later built over by the Gardeners pub.

Henry II gave Lenton Priory an eight-day fair for St Martin's Day, which Henry III lengthened to twelve, with tolls paid to the monks for every booth. The fair outlived the priory: in 1584, when servants of Mary, Queen of Scots came, it was a horse fair, and by the 17th century it was known as a great fair for all sorts of horses. In the 19th century farmers and horse dealers still came.

St Peter's, the old church of Flawford, closed in 1718 and was pulled down in 1779. Three alabaster figures found in it, probably hidden around 1539, are now at Nottingham Castle Museum, and Ruddington's chapel took its name.
The landowner John Newton built Bulwell Hall in 1770. It was sold at auction in 1864 to Samuel Thomas Cooper, and was pulled down in 1956; its grounds are now Bulwell Hall Park.

Until the Inclosure Act of 1845 the area was open Clay Fields. The Act let the town take 1,068 acres for housing, and by 1880 the streets of terraced houses called New Town were complete. The terraces north of Victoria Park are listed, as a once common kind of house now mostly lost to bombs and clearance.

Between May 1873 and November 1875 Joseph Firbank built a viaduct here for the Great Northern Railway, 43 arches and 1,716 feet long, known locally as Forty Bridges. It was pulled down in 1973 to make way for the A610 bypass.

A house called the Manor House stood here, near the river at the south end of the village green, and is said to have once been a home of the Clifton family. It appears on an 1885 map. Manor House Close was built on its site; next to it stands the only house left of the row once called Manor House and Main Road Cottages.
Cave dwellings dug into the sandstone ridge extended out into Sneinton, where they were known as the Hermitage. What little remains can still be seen along Sneinton Hermitage.

The Charlton family, after whom the Charlton Arms is named, lived at Chilwell Hall, since pulled down. In 1906 Chilwell Manor Golf Club was laid out on land that had belonged to the manor, and the Manor House and Chilwell Green stood until 1965.

Gedling's railway station closed on 4 April 1960, though coal trains ran to the colliery for decades more. Its building is now a youth centre, and there are plans to reopen the line or make it a cycleway.

The Clifton family held the manor of Clifton from the late 13th century, and this was their manor house. Sir Gervase Clifton largely rebuilt it between 1778 and 1797, partly to designs by John Carr of York. In 1958 the family sold it, ending 700 years of ownership; it became a girls' grammar school, and is now two houses. The hall itself dates from the late 16th century and is listed Grade I. In its grounds are a brick ice house of the mid-18th century, the vaulted remains of a curved garden stairway, a pair of Coade stone lions of the early 19th century, and the late 18th-century stable block, now cottages.

Before the Conquest the manor of Wilford belonged to Gode the Countess. In Domesday Book the settlement is named Willesforde, with a fishery, a priest and 23 sokemen. Clifton and Wilford, Peverel lands, passed to the Crown early in Henry II's reign, and the king granted them to Gerbode de Escalt; in Richard I's time they passed to the de Rodes family. Before 1280 Gervase de Clifton obtained both manors from Sir Gerard de Rodes for £30 a year, and a charter of 1280 confirmed the grant. In 1853 Sir J. G. J. Clifton was lord of the manor, owned all its land but the church's glebe, and was patron of the church; in 1870–72 the manor still belonged to Sir R. J. Clifton.

The Musters family gained the West Bridgford estate in 1523, reputedly by winning it in a game of cards. When they sold land for building they set strict rules for it, and the village grew into a suburb, with its own council from 1894 and part of the borough of Rushcliffe from 1972.

A local account says Sir William Clifton planted the avenue of elms in 1677, from a little stone bridge over Fairham Brook up to the hall; it was said to be wide enough for six carriages abreast. In 1853 it was "an avenue of trees a mile in length". By the 18th century the Grove was a favourite outing, and an 1874 guide tells of thousands of Nottingham artisans there at Easter and Whitsuntide. The Nottingham poet Henry Kirke White, a butcher's son, published Clifton Grove, a Sketch in Verse, in 1803, aged 17. D. H. Lawrence set a scene of Sons and Lovers (1913) in the Grove.

The red-brick dovecote on the green was built in the early 18th century for the Clifton family's farming estate. It is said to be one of the largest in England, with about 2,300 nesting places; pigeons were kept for winter meat. A stone tablet on its side remembers the men of the village who died in the First World War. It is listed Grade II.

The house was designed in 1781 for the Smith family as Wilford Hall, the centre of an estate with stables, lodges for the house staff and a private chapel. It is a red-brick country house of three storeys and five bays, listed Grade II, and its stable block of the same year is listed too. The Smiths' bank in Nottingham is believed to have been the first bank outside London, and Samuel Smith, an MP for 44 years, is believed to have built the house; by 1790 it was his. The banker Abel Smith died at Wilford on 12 July 1788. His wife's younger sister, Elizabeth Bird, was the mother of William Wilberforce, the slavery abolitionist, who stayed at the house for several months between 1786 and 1789. In 1853 it was the seat of Henry Smith, a large, handsome brick mansion; he owned about 70 acres of the parish, and in 1828 he built an infant school in the village.

Thomas Forman, who founded the Nottingham Post, later bought the house from the Smiths, and it passed to the Forman Hardy family; at some point it was renamed Wilford House. It became offices in the 1980s, the Wilford Place estate was built on its grounds in 2006, and in 2021 the house was given a multi-million pound refurbishment.

Manor House Close was built on its site; next to it stands the only house left of the row once called Manor House and Main Road Cottages.

George Fitzroy Seymour owned the estate from 1949 to 1994, and Miranda Seymour has owned it since.
Up to 1745, John Emerton of Thrumpton Hall built many of the village's gabled brick houses for the estate.

In 1860 Thomas Cross, a banker from Bolton, built the hall. From 1880 it was the home of Philo Laos Mills, an American merchant who became High Sheriff of Nottinghamshire. In the Second World War it became a hospital, and it stayed one until 1980.

The Charlton family, after whom the Charlton Arms is named, lived at Chilwell Hall, since pulled down. In 1906 Chilwell Manor Golf Club was laid out on land that had belonged to the manor, and the Manor House and Chilwell Green stood until 1965.

The Pierreponts held Holme from about 1280. Around 1500 the hall was built, one of the few brick houses of its time in Nottinghamshire. The family became Earls and Dukes of Kingston, then Earls Manvers, and the hall is listed Grade I.

In November 1645 Parliament's troops under Sydnam Poyntz, with Colonel John Hutchinson leading the assault, stormed Shelford House, held for the King by Philip Stanhope. About 160 of its defenders were killed, and the house was burnt that night.

In 1948 the Roman Catholic Diocese of Nottingham opened St Hugh's College at Tollerton Hall, a junior seminary for boys from 11. By 1969 it was taking boys who were not training for the priesthood, and it closed in 1986. The hall was then a company's headquarters until 2017, when it was bought as a private home again. It is listed Grade II.

When the House of Lords threw out the Second Reform Bill on 8 October 1831, rioting broke out in Nottingham and a crowd burned the castle, which belonged to the Duke of Newcastle, an opponent of reform. Three men were hanged; the Duke refused to restore the castle, and its burnt shell stood on the rock for years.

In the 1790s Ichabod Wright built Mapperley Hall at the heart of his estate. His grandson, Colonel Charles Ichabod Wright, began selling land for houses in 1873, but most of the estate was released only in 1903; some 163 houses were approved in Mapperley Park between 1906 and 1914.

In 1854 the Duke's estate took on the Nottingham architect Thomas Chambers Hine, to design many of the Park's villas. The roads are still lit by gas lamps, believed to be one of the largest such networks left in Europe.
Henry Ashwell, a Basford bleacher, built Woodthorpe Grange in 1874. The council bought the house and grounds in 1921 for £15,000, Jesse Boot giving £5,000 of it, and the park opened in 1922.

links.text: The 8th Duke of Newcastle sold the Park in 1938 to the Nuffield Trust, which passed it on to Oxford University. The estate became a conservation area in 1969, and talks that began in 1986 between the residents' association and the university put the estate in the hands of its residents, who run it from the Estate Office.

Sir Francis Willoughby built Wollaton Hall between 1580 and 1588, probably to designs by the Elizabethan architect Robert Smythson. After a fire in 1642 the house stood empty for some forty years; Wyatville remodelled it from 1801. The 11th Baron Middleton sold it to Nottingham Corporation for £200,000, and since it opened to the public in 1926 it has held the city's natural history museum.
The landowner John Newton built Bulwell Hall in 1770. It was sold at auction in 1864 to Samuel Thomas Cooper, and was pulled down in 1956; its grounds are now Bulwell Hall Park.
Papplewick Hall was built between 1781 and 1787 for the Hon. Frederick Montagu, and in 1795 the church of St James was built in its grounds.

The first written record of a royal hunting lodge at Bestwood is from 1286, in the reign of Edward I. Charles II and Nell Gwyn visited it, and in 1682 he leased the lodge to her. Their son, Charles Beauclerk, Earl of Burford, was made Duke of St Albans in 1684, and Bestwood passed down through his descendants.

On the night of 8–9 May 1941 the Luftwaffe bombed Nottingham. Firefighters saved St Mary's Church after an incendiary burned through its roof; three Boots factories, in Poplar Street, Island Street and Station Street, were on fire; University College and the Shakespeare Street chapel were hit. The worst loss was at the Co-op bakery on Meadow Lane, where 49 people died. In all, 159 people were killed that night.
A church was built here in the 12th century, and it is listed Grade II*. In 1894 Arthur Brewill and Basil Baily rebuilt its chancel, and its east window has glass by Morris & Co.

A church was built here in the 13th century. George Edmund Street restored it in 1871, and it is listed Grade II*.
A church was built here in the 14th century. Altered over the centuries, it was restored in 1877 and 1885, and it is listed Grade I.

links.text: A medieval church stood here, though little of it remains; it keeps a screen from the late 14th century. Thomas Chambers Hine restored it in 1872, and in 1896 a new nave and chancel were begun, their foundation stone laid by Lady Byron of Thrumpton Hall.

Around 1361 Gervase de Wilford is thought to have founded a church here, and the building dates from the late 14th century; it was restored in 1890–92 by Naylor and Sale. Inside are two memorials to the poet Henry Kirke White, who drew much inspiration from Wilford and Clifton.

A church of St Nicholas stood here from the 11th or 12th century. In the Civil War, Royalists took its tower and fired on the castle's garrison, so in 1643 the castle's governor, Colonel John Hutchinson, had it destroyed. For 28 years there was no church here; the brick church standing today was begun in 1671 and finished in 1678.

In 1837 the present church was built to Thomas Rickman's design. Between 1909 and 1912 it was extended to designs by George Frederick Bodley.
Building began in 1841 on a Catholic church designed by Augustus Pugin, with much of the cost paid by Lord Shrewsbury. It was consecrated in 1844, and in 1852 it became a cathedral.

The church of St Ann was begun for the new district in the 1860s: Sydney Pierrepont, 3rd Earl Manvers, laid its foundation stone on 23 September 1863, and it was consecrated on 26 September 1864, a daughter church of St Mary's. The parish church today is St Ann with Emmanuel. Whether the 1864 church stood here is not known.

The congregation went back to 1690 and became Unitarian in 1802. In 1876 it built this chapel, to designs by Stuart Colman. Worship ended in 1982; the chapel then housed a lace museum, and it is now a Pitcher & Piano.

William Booth, who founded the Salvation Army, was born in Sneinton on 10 April 1829. At 13 he was apprenticed to a pawnbroker. His birthplace is now a museum.
The building began in 1839 as a grand Wesleyan chapel on Broad Street. Broadway opened here in 1990, and one of its screens is the only cinema screen designed by Sir Paul Smith.

The first Albert Hall, a temperance hall by Watson Fothergill, opened in 1876 and from 1902 was a Wesleyan Methodist mission; it burnt down on 22 April 1906. Albert Edward Lambert designed the present hall, dedicated in 1909, and it stayed a Methodist mission until 1982. It is now a conference and concert venue.

The Anglo-Saxon cross in St Helen's churchyard dates from around AD 1000, though some put it as early as the 8th century. Its shaft is carved with interlace and a winged figure with a spear, perhaps an archangel or St Luke. Its head was lost in the 18th century; after several moves it came to the churchyard in 1928. Pevsner called it by far the most important pre-Conquest monument in Nottinghamshire, and it is listed Grade I.

The village appears as Calvretone in the Domesday survey of 1086, with a church and a priest. St Wilfrid's Church dates mostly from the 14th century; its nave and tower were rebuilt in 1760–63 and its chancel in 1835, and it was restored in 1881.
St Peter's dates from the end of the 12th century; work in 1909 gave it the shape it has today. It is listed Grade II.
All Saints' Church dates from the 12th century, with later alterations and additions. An arson attack in 1996 did it great damage.

Domesday Book calls the village Aitone. Its church of St Laurence stands east of the Market Place: local tradition dates parts of it to the 11th century and King Cnut, but its oldest parts may be from after the Conquest, in the 12th century. It was a daughter church of Sawley until the 19th century. It is listed Grade II*.
Arnold's parish church of St Mary is believed to date from 1176. It is listed Grade II*.

St Lawrence's dates from the 13th century; it was restored in 1789 and repaired in 1869, and Reuben Bosworth made its tower clock in 1848 for £70. Among its memorials is one to John St Andrew and his wife, of 1625. It is listed Grade I.
The old village of Wollaton gathers round two buildings: the church of St Leonard, which goes back to the 13th century, and the Admiral Rodney pub. The church is listed Grade II*.

All Hallows Church dates from the 13th century. It was restored in 1872, and its roof in 1892 by Arthur Blomfield. Its tall, thin broach spire has two tiers of lucarnes and a weathercock, and the church is listed Grade I.
Around 1292–94 a manor chapel, St Mary's, was founded in the village. It took the name of St Peter's from the old parish church at Flawford when that was pulled down in the 1770s.

By 1310–11 Shelford's church belonged to an Augustinian priory here. After Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries, the Stanhopes acquired the priory, in 1537, and with it the church. Lady Anne Stanhope's tomb, by Gabriel Royle, was put up after her death in 1588, and the family vault is dated 1677. In 1877–78 Lord Carnarvon paid for Ewan Christian to restore the church.

links.text: St Helen's was given its clerestory towards the end of the 15th century. Its monuments include Robert Tevery, who died in 1571, and Gervase Tevery, who died in 1639. A classical porch was added in 1785, the church was restored in 1875–77, and a memorial chapel came in 1923. It is listed Grade II*.

Henry Pierrepont, 1st Marquess of Dorchester, largely rebuilt the medieval church in 1666, and in 1878 T. C. Hine added its chancel. Its monuments remember the Pierreponts, from Sir Henry, who died in 1499, onwards, and the satirical poet John Oldham. It is listed Grade I.
William Peveril gave Radford's church of St Peter to Lenton Priory. The church was rebuilt in 1812 at a cost of £2,000, and is listed Grade II.
Storms in 1843 damaged the old church of St Mary beyond repair, and a new one was built on its site in 1849–50 to the designs of Henry Isaac Stevens. It is listed Grade II.

The tower of St Leodegarius fell in 1859; Thomas Allom designed the new one, and the church reopened on 1 March 1860. A fire on 29 November 1900 closed it again until 24 April 1902. It is listed Grade II*.
