links.text: St Jude's on Woodborough Road opened in 1877 on land given by the Wright family, as a daughter church of St Ann's. Its chancel came in 1893 and its aisles in 1916, and it became a parish of its own on 9 November 1926.
Henry Herbert, 4th Earl of Carnarvon, built the church of St Paul, which was consecrated in 1885. It is listed Grade II.
Christ Church was built in 1903 for Chilwell's growing population. It became a parish of its own, apart from Attenborough, in 1975.

Their datestone reads "George Wells, Anno 1709", though Wells's will was written in 1712. The almshouses were for six poor unmarried or widowed women, kept up by his lands in Cropwell Bishop, Wilford and Ruddington, with Sir Gervase Clifton and his heirs as trustees; each woman had an allowance and three tons of coal a year from Clifton Colliery. Restored in the 1970s, they are now two homes.

links.text: The "fools of Gotham" were already mentioned in the fifteenth century, in the Towneley plays. A legend says that the villagers played the fool, even trying to fence in a cuckoo, so that King John would build his road and hunting lodge elsewhere. In 1807 Washington Irving called New York "Gotham", and Batman's Gotham City took the name.

A ballad, Bateman's Tragedy, tells of a young man, Bateman, and a beautiful heiress of Clifton who pledge to marry; she breaks her word for a richer widower, and on her wedding day he hangs himself at her door. His ghost haunts her, and in the end carries her off. In the version told locally, the jilted lover drowns himself in the Trent and the bride is dragged into the river at the chasm in the Grove; in another, a Clifton beauty is murdered and thrown down the cliff.

In 1804–05 the young poet Henry Kirke White lived at Wilford Crossroads. He is said to have spent much of his time writing poems in the churchyard, under his favourite tree.
Gotham means "goat home" in Old English. Washington Irving gave the name "Gotham" to New York in his Salmagundi Papers of 1807, and Bill Finger in turn named Batman's city Gotham City.

links.text: In 1836 the young Nottingham poet Philip James Bailey went to live at his father's house in Old Basford to write. The result was Festus, a vast poem on the Faust story published in 1839, which Tennyson admired.

Built in 1877–81 for University College Nottingham, with the town's library and a natural history museum, and damaged by bombs in the Second World War. D. H. Lawrence studied here to become a teacher; it is now Nottingham Trent University's Arkwright Building.
28 Garden Road, a brick miner's cottage of about 1880 at the end of a row, was another of the Lawrences' homes. It is listed Grade II.
D. H. Lawrence was born in 1885 at 8a Victoria Street, a brick house of about 1875 and one of the four houses his family lived in in Eastwood. It became a museum in 1976, and is listed Grade II.

Alan Sillitoe's 1958 novel became a 1960 film directed by Karel Reisz, with Albert Finney as Arthur Seaton, who works at the Raleigh factory. Much of the exterior location filming took place in Nottingham, and shooting at a Nottingham factory ran two days over schedule and £3,500 over budget.

Garners Hill, said to be the oldest site in Nottingham, once held cave dwellings, a Saxon fort and a medieval town hall, until the Victorians cleared it for a railway line. On 14 November 2009 an art centre designed by Caruso St John opened here, its walls embossed with a Nottingham lace pattern.

The inn stood by the bridge before any cricket was played here. The cricketer William Clarke married its landlady, Mary Chapman, and in 1838 they had the field behind it cleared and fenced for the first match on what became Trent Bridge. Clarke left for London in 1845, and his stepson John Chapman ran the pub and the ground. After the First World War the Musters family, who owned both, sold them to the cricket club.
The first recorded match was played on ground behind the Trent Bridge Inn in 1838, and William Clarke opened the ground in 1841. It hosted its first Test match, England against Australia, in 1899.
The first Test at Trent Bridge, England against Australia in June 1899, was W. G. Grace's last Test and Wilfred Rhodes's first.

links.text: Bodyline, fast bowling aimed at the batsman's body, was England's tactic in the Ashes in Australia in 1932–33. Its bowlers were Nottinghamshire's Harold Larwood and Bill Voce, whom Douglas Jardine met with their county captain, Arthur Carr, to plan it. The uproar ended Larwood's Test career and changed the laws of cricket; Trent Bridge opened the Larwood and Voce Stand in 1985.
Nottingham's racecourse by 1773, and the ground where a club formed in 1865 first played, taking its name from it: Nottingham Forest. Goose Fair has been held here since 1928.

Notts County, called the oldest professional football club in the world, gives 1862 as its foundation, though it was formally organised on 7 December 1864. Its first recorded matches were at the Meadows Cricket Ground, its home until October 1877. It played at Trent Bridge from 1883, and since 1910 at Meadow Lane, on land leased from Nottingham Corporation. In 1894 it beat Bolton Wanderers 4–1 at Goodison Park, the first Second Division team to win the FA Cup. Late in 1901 a set of Notts-style kits sent to Turin gave Juventus their black and white stripes.

Nottingham Forest moved here in 1898, to their seventh home. The name dates from 1897, when Nottingham was granted city status, and Notts County's Meadow Lane is only three hundred yards away, on the other side of the Trent.
On 16 April 1898, at the Crystal Palace in south London, Nottingham Forest beat Derby County 3–1. It was the first FA Cup final for both clubs.
Notts County moved here on 3 September 1910. Divided by the Trent, Meadow Lane and the City Ground are the closest pair of football grounds in England.

Brian Clough managed Nottingham Forest from January 1975 to May 1993. Under him the club won the League in 1977–78 and the European Cup in 1979 and 1980. Les Johnson's statue of him, at the corner of King Street and Queen Street, was unveiled by his widow Barbara on 6 November 2008.

Under Brian Clough, Nottingham Forest won the European Cup in Munich in May 1979, beating Malmö 1–0 with a goal by Trevor Francis, and again in Madrid a year later, beating Hamburg 1–0 with a goal by John Robertson: back-to-back European Cups.
The Cadland inn is named after the racehorse that won the Derby in 1828.
Dug out of a former gravel works, the centre opened in 1971, and hosted the World Rowing Championships in 1975 and 1986. Its whitewater course was built in 1986.

Three men were hanged; the Duke refused to restore the castle, and its burnt shell stood on the rock for years.

In 1995 the Design Museum in London put on True Brit, a show marking 25 years of the fashion business of Paul Smith, who was born in Beeston. It went on to Glasgow and then to his home city, where it was shown in Nottingham Castle.
In August 1642 Charles I raised his standard outside Nottingham Castle, at the opening of the English Civil War.
Henry Poole's bronze of the airman Albert Ball, with an allegorical female figure, in the castle gardens. Ball was killed on 7 May 1917, and the memorial was unveiled in 1921; it is listed Grade I.

When George Larpent resigned his Nottingham seat, Joseph Sturge stood at the by-election: a reformer whose Complete Suffrage Union, a more middle-class rival to the Chartists' own association, campaigned for votes for all men. He lost, and the Conservative John Walter was elected on 4 August 1842; Walter was unseated on petition the next year, and the Liberal Thomas Gisborne won the seat in April 1843. Five years later Nottingham elected the Chartist leader Feargus O'Connor. Where the poll was held is not known.

links.text: Brian Clough managed Nottingham Forest from January 1975 to May 1993. Under him the club won the League in 1977–78 and the European Cup in 1979 and 1980. Les Johnson's statue of him, at the corner of King Street and Queen Street, was unveiled by his widow Barbara on 6 November 2008.
A hotel on Long Row, rebuilt in 1886–88 by Watson Fothergill and enlarged around 1900. It was demolished in 1970, and a new shop building, first Littlewoods, went up in its place.

The first Albert Hall, a temperance hall by Watson Fothergill, opened in 1876 and from 1902 was a Wesleyan Methodist mission; it burnt down on 22 April 1906. Albert Edward Lambert designed the present hall, dedicated in 1909, and it stayed a Methodist mission until 1982. It is now a conference and concert venue.

John Leavers lived here, at Canning Circus, where a plaque calls him the inventor of the Leavers lace machine, in 1813. He improved John Heathcoat's lace machine, and in 1821 emigrated to Grand-Couronne in Normandy.
The stone statue of Feargus O'Connor, by J. B. Robinson of Derby, went up in the Arboretum in 1859: the Chartist leader whom Nottingham had elected its MP in 1847. It is listed Grade II.

Joseph Else's memorial to Samuel Morley, of bronze and stone, stands at the Arboretum's Waverley Street entrance: the hosier who was elected the town's MP in 1865. The list of the city's public art dates it to 1928. It is listed Grade II.

links.text: The Representation of the People Act, passed on 6 February 1918, gave the vote to women of 30 and over who met a property qualification, and they voted for the first time on 14 December 1918. That November women had also been allowed to stand for Parliament: in Nottinghamshire the first to do so was Violet Markham, at Mansfield, who lost. In 1919 Bridgid Burke-Bloor became the first woman to stand for Nottingham City Council, and in 1920 Helena Dowson and Caroline Harper were its first women councillors. Women won the vote on the same terms as men on 2 July 1928. A hundred years to the day after that first vote, the city unveiled a plaque by a juniper tree in the Arboretum for the suffragette Helen Watts.

On 11 November 1927 a memorial designed by the City Engineer Thomas Wallis Gordon was unveiled on land beside the Trent given by Sir Jesse Boot. It remembers the men of Nottingham who died in both World Wars.
Richard Arkwright's first cotton mill opened in Nottingham in 1768, its machines turned by horses. By 1772 it had four storeys and 300 workers.

John Boot opened a herbalist's shop on Goose Gate in 1849, and his son Jesse was born in the area, into poverty, the next year. After John died in 1860 his widow Mary kept the shop going as M & J Boot. Jesse became a partner at 21, and in 1883 he built a larger store on the same site, the first of the Boots shops; Nottingham Civic Society put up a plaque here in 2015.

In 1854 the Duke's estate took on the Nottingham architect Thomas Chambers Hine, to design many of the Park's villas. The roads are still lit by gas lamps, believed to be one of the largest such networks left in Europe.
In 1804–05 the young poet Henry Kirke White lived at Wilford Crossroads. He is said to have spent much of his time writing poems in the churchyard, under his favourite tree.
The first recorded match was played on ground behind the Trent Bridge Inn in 1838, and William Clarke opened the ground in 1841. It hosted its first Test match, England against Australia, in 1899.

The inn stood by the bridge before any cricket was played here. The cricketer William Clarke married its landlady, Mary Chapman, and in 1838 they had the field behind it cleared and fenced for the first match on what became Trent Bridge. Clarke left for London in 1845, and his stepson John Chapman ran the pub and the ground. After the First World War the Musters family, who owned both, sold them to the cricket club.
The first Test at Trent Bridge, England against Australia in June 1899, was W. G. Grace's last Test and Wilfred Rhodes's first.

A medieval church stood here, though little of it remains; it keeps a screen from the late 14th century. Thomas Chambers Hine restored it in 1872, and in 1896 a new nave and chancel were begun, their foundation stone laid by Lady Byron of Thrumpton Hall.

A local account says Sir William Clifton planted the avenue of elms in 1677, from a little stone bridge over Fairham Brook up to the hall; it was said to be wide enough for six carriages abreast. In 1853 it was "an avenue of trees a mile in length". By the 18th century the Grove was a favourite outing, and an 1874 guide tells of thousands of Nottingham artisans there at Easter and Whitsuntide. Henry Pierrepont, 1st Marquess of Dorchester, largely rebuilt the medieval church in 1666, and in 1878 T. C. Hine added its chancel. Its monuments remember the Pierreponts, from Sir Henry, who died in 1499, onwards, and the satirical poet John Oldham. It is listed Grade I.

When Parliament's forces took Shelford House on 3 November 1645, Royalists led by a woman fired on them from the church tower; John Hutchinson had straw set alight to smoke them out, and smoke stains in the tower stairwell may date from then. Lady Anne Stanhope's monument and the font were damaged; the font was replaced in 1662.

links.text: In November 1645 Parliament's troops under Sydnam Poyntz, with Colonel John Hutchinson leading the assault, stormed Shelford House, held for the King by Philip Stanhope. About 160 of its defenders were killed, and the house was burnt that night.
In 1885 a small bicycle workshop opened in Raleigh Street and gave the company its name; Frank Bowden took it over in 1888.

John Player built his Castle Tobacco Factories in Radford, and the firm's three bonded warehouses, seven to nine storeys high, were finished here in 1939. Tobacco making in Nottingham ended in 2016; the warehouses were demolished, the last in 2022.

Alan Sillitoe's 1958 novel became a 1960 film directed by Karel Reisz, with Albert Finney as Arthur Seaton, who works at the Raleigh factory. Much of the exterior location filming took place in Nottingham, and shooting at a Nottingham factory ran two days over schedule and £3,500 over budget.

Thomas Humber started making bicycles in Nottingham, and around 1878 moved the business to Beeston, where a new works was built for it. The firm later had works in Coventry and Wolverhampton too.

Viscount Chetwynd built the factory from 1915 to fill shells with explosive; it filled some 19 million during the First World War. On 1 July 1918 eight tons of TNT exploded, killing 134 people. The site is now Chetwynd Barracks.
D. H. Lawrence was born in 1885 at 8a Victoria Street, a brick house of about 1875 and one of the four houses his family lived in in Eastwood. It became a museum in 1976, and is listed Grade II.

Henry Ireton, eldest son of German Ireton of Attenborough, was baptised in St Mary's Church here on 3 November 1611. He fought for Parliament at Edgehill in October 1642. On the night before Naseby, in June 1645, he surprised the Royalist army; the next day he was wounded and captured, and Cromwell later freed him. He married Bridget, Cromwell's eldest daughter, was one of the commissioners who signed the death warrant of Charles I, and died of disease outside Limerick on 26 November 1651.

In 1589 William Lee of Calverton invented the stocking frame, a machine that knitted. Legend has it that Elizabeth I refused him a patent. The trade grew here, and from 1728 Nottingham was one of its main centres.

In 1881–84 a pumping station was built here to raise drinking water for Nottingham from deep wells. It had two beam engines by James Watt & Co. and an engine house by Marriott Ogle Tarbotton, ornate with cast iron and stained glass. It pumped until 1969 and opened as a museum in 1976.

St Mary Magdalene's stands on the site of a Saxon church. Its tower was built in stages between the 12th and 14th centuries, and its porch in 1320. Most of the Lords Byron lie in the family vault here, among them the poet Lord Byron, and his daughter Ada, Countess of Lovelace, rests there too. links.text: In 1836 the young Nottingham poet Philip James Bailey went to live at his father's house in Old Basford to write. The result was Festus, a vast poem on the Faust story published in 1839, which Tennyson admired.
Storms in 1843 damaged the old church of St Mary beyond repair, and a new one was built on its site in 1849–50 to the designs of Henry Isaac Stevens. It is listed Grade II.
Henry Ashwell, a Basford bleacher, built Woodthorpe Grange in 1874. The council bought the house and grounds in 1921 for £15,000, Jesse Boot giving £5,000 of it, and the park opened in 1922.

links.text: T. C. Hine designed the Coppice Hospital, a hospital on the hill off Ransom Road, built in 1857–59. It closed in 1985, and the building is now flats.

Lucy Hutchinson, born in the Tower of London in 1620, was the first to translate the whole of Lucretius into English verse, and her Order and Disorder is perhaps the first epic poem by a woman in English. Her life of her husband, John Hutchinson, written for her family, was printed in 1806. She died at Owthorpe in 1681.
William Howitt, born in Heanor, made his home in Nottingham with Mary Howitt and was an alderman of the town, before they moved to Esher in 1837. In 1852 he sailed to Melbourne with two of his sons.

Mary Howitt married William Howitt in 1821, and by 1823 they were living in Nottingham, on Timber Hill, now South Parade, next to Smith's Bank, for over twelve years. She wrote The Spider and the Fly and translated Hans Christian Andersen's tales.

Florence Boot, born in St Helier, Jersey, in 1863, married Jesse Boot in 1886 and helped him run the firm. She brought books and stationery into the Goose Gate shop and started Boots Book-Lovers' Library and cafés in the stores. She founded the university's first hall for women, named Florence Boot Hall after her.

James Iremonger was born in Norton, in the East Riding of Yorkshire, on 5 March 1876, and played for Wilford's football club in 1893. He played for Nottingham Forest from 1895 to 1910, won two England caps in 1901–02, played cricket for Nottinghamshire from 1899 to 1914 and coached the county from 1921 to 1938. His brother was Albert Iremonger, the Notts County goalkeeper. He died in Nottingham on 25 March 1956.

Harold Larwood, born at Nuncargate in 1904, played for Nottinghamshire from 1924 and bowled for England in the Bodyline series. He moved to Australia in 1950; Trent Bridge named the Larwood and Voce Stand after him and Bill Voce in 1985.
Bill Voce, born at Annesley Woodhouse in 1909, walked from Hucknall to Trent Bridge hoping for a trial. With Harold Larwood he bowled Bodyline for England, and he later became the county's coach.

The Clifton family held the manor of Clifton from the late 13th century, and this was their manor house. Sir Gervase Clifton largely rebuilt it between 1778 and 1797, partly to designs by John Carr of York. In 1958 the family sold it, ending 700 years of ownership; it became a girls' grammar school, and is now two houses. The hall itself dates from the late 16th century and is listed Grade I. In its grounds are a brick ice house of the mid-18th century, the vaulted remains of a curved garden stairway, a pair of Coade stone lions of the early 19th century, and the late 18th-century stable block, now cottages.

The first house in the park, built in 1809 opposite the castle gatehouse, was the vicarage of St Mary's. In 1827 the architect Peter Frederick Robinson published a plan for building over the park, and houses began to go up along Park Terrace in about 1829; within three years there were 40 to 50 of them.

A legacy from the banker John Key paid for a hospital on part of Nottingham Park. Its first building, designed by John Simpson, was begun on 12 February 1781 and opened with 44 beds in September 1782; John Wesley was an early visitor. In 1844 it took in the hurt when a stand collapsed at a hanging on Garner's Hill, killing twelve. Hine added a storey in 1855, and Alfred Waterhouse's round Jubilee Wing opened in 1900. It closed in 1992, its work moved to the Queen's Medical Centre.
In 1836 a cemetery of 18 acres was established at the top of Sion Hill, now Canning Circus, with a gatehouse and almshouses by Samuel Sutton Rawlinson. More than 150,000 people are buried here.

Watson Fothergill, born Fothergill Watson, took his mother's family name in 1892 and built his own offices here, on George Street, in 1895. Its front has a statue of a medieval architect and busts of Augustus Pugin and George Edmund Street; it is listed Grade II.
The church dates from about 1190, and is listed Grade I. Lewis Nockalls Cottingham restored it in 1846, and much of the decoration is by George Frederick Bodley.

Its cupola held a bell that British troops took from a temple in Canton during the Second Opium War, until the bell went to the regimental museum in 1956. Two of the cannon beside it were taken at Sebastopol in the Crimean War; the other two are copies.

Phipps; its portico of six Corinthian columns closes the view up Market Street. It opened on 25 September 1865 with Sheridan's The School for Scandal, and in 1897 Frank Matcham remodelled its auditorium.

In 1898 Frank Matcham designed and built the Empire Palace of Varieties here. It closed for the last time in 1958 and was demolished for road-widening in 1969. On 27 November 1982 the Royal Concert Hall, designed by the Renton Howard Wood Levin Partnership, opened on the site, with Elton John as its first performer.

Nottingham's first station, opened in 1839 by the Midland Counties Railway, stood across Carrington Street; a through station replaced it on this site in 1848. The present building, of red brick and terracotta, was designed by the local architect Albert Edward Lambert and opened on 16 January 1904.
A church was built here in the 12th century, and it is listed Grade II*. In 1894 Arthur Brewill and Basil Baily rebuilt its chancel, and its east window has glass by Morris & Co.

In 1643 Colonel John Hutchinson took command of Nottingham Castle, and Parliament later made him governor of both town and castle. It was a hard post: the town had no walls, the garrison was small and short of supplies, and the committee that ran the town quarrelled. Hutchinson held on all the same, and protected the radical separatists among his soldiers as far as he could.

A church of St Nicholas stood here from the 11th or 12th century. In the Civil War, Royalists took its tower and fired on the castle's garrison, so in 1643 the castle's governor, Colonel John Hutchinson, had it destroyed. For 28 years there was no church here; the brick church standing today was begun in 1671 and finished in 1678.

Pierrepont is Norman French for "stone bridge". In 1257 Sir Henry Pierrepont married Annora de Manvers, heir to Holme, and the family stayed for almost seven centuries: Charles I made Sir Robert Pierrepont Earl of Kingston-upon-Hull in 1628, and George I made Evelyn Pierrepont a duke in 1715. The estate was broken up and sold in 1940.

The first written record of a royal hunting lodge at Bestwood is from 1286, in the reign of Edward I. Charles II and Nell Gwyn visited it, and in 1682 he leased the lodge to her. Their son, Charles Beauclerk, Earl of Burford, was made Duke of St Albans in 1684, and Bestwood passed down through his descendants.
